findings.explanation: At line 299, both `key` and `value` are interpolated directly into a raw SQL string passed to SQLAlchemy's `text()` function using Python's `.format()`. The `key` variable originates from user-supplied filter input (a dictionary key parsed from a string or passed directly by callers) that was only coerced to a model attribute when it matches a known model class attribute — but for JSON column paths (the `elif json_column:` branch at line 291), the key is left as a plain string (not a model attribute) and is never sanitised or validated against a whitelist before interpolation. The `value` variable is typecasted in `_try_typecast_string` but if it remains a string (e.g. an arbitrary user-supplied metadata value), it is interpolated verbatim into the SQL fragment. No bound parameters / placeholders are used: the resulting expression is `text("json_exists(meta,'$?(@.<key> == \"<value>\")')")` where `<key>` and `<value>` are attacker-controlled strings. An attacker can craft a filter key or value that breaks out of the JSON path expression and injects arbitrary Oracle SQL.

evidence.content: expression = text("json_exists(meta,'$?(@.{} == \"{}\")'))" .format(key, value))
expression = text("json_exists(meta,'$?(@.{} == \"{}\")')".format(key, value))
fe = FilterEngine(filters, model_class=models.DidMeta, strict_coerce=False)
expression = text("json_exists(meta,'$?(@.{} == \"{}\")') ".format(key, value))

findings.suggested_fix:
Replace the string interpolation with bound parameters. For Oracle's `json_exists`, pass the key as a validated identifier (check against an explicit whitelist of allowed metadata keys) and bind the value as a named parameter, e.g.:

```python
# Validate key against a whitelist or sanitise it
if not re.match(r'^[a-zA-Z0-9_]+$', key):
    raise exception.FilterEngineGenericError("Invalid metadata key.")
expression = text("json_exists(meta,'$?(@." + key + " == :val)')").bindparams(val=value)
```
The `key` (JSON path attribute name) cannot be a bound parameter in Oracle JSON path syntax, so it must be strictly validated against an allowlist of known safe attribute names. The `value` must be passed as a bound parameter using `.bindparams()` rather than via `.format()`.
findings.semgrep_message: SQLAlchemy text()/exec_driver_sql() with dynamic content may allow SQL injection if user input is interpolated. Verify that only bound parameters are used.

findings.explanation: In the PR, when a filter group contains a 'scope' key, line 109 incorrectly writes the InternalScope value into or_group['account'] instead of or_group['scope']. This means the 'scope' filter key is never converted to its VO-prefixed internal representation before being passed to the core query layer. As a result, the raw external scope string (without the VO prefix, e.g. 'myscope' instead of 'myscope@vo1') reaches the database query. In a multi-VO deployment, InternalScope and InternalAccount embed the VO prefix (e.g. 'value@vo') to enforce VO isolation. Skipping this conversion for the 'scope' filter allows a user from one VO to supply a raw scope value that may match records belonging to a different VO, effectively bypassing the VO-boundary authorization enforced by the InternalScope/InternalAccount internalization pattern used throughout the API layer.

findings.suggested_fix: Change line 109 from `or_group['account'] = InternalScope(or_group['scope'], vo=vo)` to `or_group['scope'] = InternalScope(or_group['scope'], vo=vo)` so that the scope filter value is correctly stored back under the 'scope' key with the VO-prefixed internal representation, matching the pattern used for the 'account' key on line 107.

findings.explanation: In `_coerce_filter_word_to_model_attribute` (line 86-92), a user-supplied filter key string (`word`) is mapped to a SQLAlchemy model attribute via `hasattr`/`getattr` with no allowlist of permitted column names. This means any attribute name that exists on the model class — including internal, sensitive, or metadata attributes (e.g. `__table__`, `__mapper__`, `_sa_class_manager`, or any column not intended to be user-queryable) — can be directly resolved and included in a database query. The `strict=True` mode only blocks attributes that do NOT exist on the model, which is the opposite of what an allowlist-based control would do. The PR introduces this method and the `strict_coerce` parameter pathway, which is a new exposure: previously the filter translation did not use this dynamic `getattr` pattern. This allows a user to filter (and thus enumerate or probe) on columns that should not be accessible — an incorrect authorization check that gates access only on attribute existence rather than on explicit permission.

findings.suggested_fix: Introduce an explicit allowlist of permitted filter key names (e.g. a class-level or module-level set of approved column names) and validate `word` against that allowlist before calling `getattr`. Reject any key not in the allowlist regardless of whether it exists as a model attribute. This prevents users from probing or filtering on internal, sensitive, or unintended columns.

findings.explanation: The new `_coerce_filter_word_to_model_attribute` method uses `hasattr`/`getattr` to map any user-supplied filter key string to any attribute of the SQLAlchemy model class. There is no allowlist restricting which model attributes users may reference. This means a user can supply a key matching any column on the model (e.g. internal audit fields, password hashes, tokens, or other sensitive columns) and have that column included in the query's SELECT and WHERE clauses, potentially exposing data the user should not be able to filter on or retrieve.
findings.suggested_fix: Maintain an explicit allowlist of permitted filter keys for each model class. In `_coerce_filter_word_to_model_attribute`, validate `word` against this allowlist before calling `getattr`, and raise `KeyNotFound` for any key not on the allowlist, regardless of whether the model actually has that attribute.

findings.explanation: The PR replaces a static allowlist (`HARDCODED_KEYS`) with a dynamic denylist approach in `manages_key`. It introspects all columns of `models.DataIdentifier` at runtime and subtracts a hardcoded exclusion list. The `_coerce_filter_word_to_model_attribute` method then uses `hasattr`/`getattr` on the model class with user-supplied filter key strings (filter_engine.py lines 87-88). If any sensitive column is missing from `exclude_did_table_columns` (e.g. due to future model additions), users can supply that column name as a filter key and probe or infer data about DIDs they may not own, constituting an IDOR via unintended attribute exposure. The previous base code used an explicit allowlist (`HARDCODED_KEYS`) which was safe-by-default; the new denylist is unsafe-by-default.

evidence.content:
def manages_key(self, key, session=None):
        all_did_table_columns = []
        for column in inspect(models.DataIdentifier).attrs:
            all_did_table_columns.append(column.key)

        exclude_did_table_columns = [
            'account',
            'availability',
            'complete',
            'created_at',
            'did_type',
            'is_open',
            'monotonic',
            'obsolete',
            'scope',
            'suppressed',
            'updated_at'
        ]
        ...
        hardcoded_keys = list(set(all_did_table_columns) - set(exclude_did_table_columns)) + additional_keys

        return key in hardcoded_keys

findings.suggested_fix: Revert `manages_key` to use an explicit allowlist of permitted filter keys (as was done with `HARDCODED_KEYS` in the base), rather than a denylist computed from all model columns minus exclusions. This ensures that new model columns added in the future are not automatically exposed as user-filterable attributes without a deliberate security review.

[README.rst:1-29] (relevance 0.12)
Rucio - Scientific Data Management
==================================

Rucio is a software framework that provides functionality to organize, manage, and access large volumes of scientific data using customisable policies. The data can be spread across globally distributed locations and across heterogeneous data centers, uniting different storage and network technologies as a single federated entity. Rucio offers advanced features such as distributed data recovery or adaptive replication, and is highly scalable, modular, and extensible. Rucio has been originally developed to meet the requirements of the high-energy physics experiment ATLAS, and is continuously extended to support LHC experiments and other diverse scientific communities.

Documentation
-------------

General information, API/REST description and guides can be found in our `documentation <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation>`_ or on our `webpage <https://rucio.cern.ch>`_.

Try it out
----------

We provide a `dockerized environment <https://github.com/rucio/rucio/tree/master/etc/docker/dev>`_ which serves both as a demo environment and a development environment. It includes all the necessary preconfigured components for multiple storage and transfers developments.

Developers
----------

For information on how to contribute to Rucio, please refer and follow our `CONTRIBUTING <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation/contributing>`_ guidelines. We strongly recommend to use the `dockerized environment <https://github.com/rucio/rucio/tree/master/etc/docker/dev>`_ for development.

Operators
----------

To learn how to deploy and configure Rucio, consult the `documentation <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation>`_ available online.

Getting Support
----------------

If you are looking for support, join us on our Slack `support <https://rucio.slack.com/messages/#support>`_ channel, or send an email to our public mailing list `rucio-users@googlegroups.com <mailto:rucio-users@googlegroups.com>`_.

Operators
----------

To learn how to deploy and configure Rucio, consult the `documentation <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation>`_ available online.

Getting Support
----------------

If you are looking for support, join us on our Slack `support <https://rucio.slack.com/messages/#support>`_ channel, or send an email to our public mailing list `rucio-users@googlegroups.com <mailto:rucio-users@googlegroups.com>`_.

Then you will have to run the transfer daemons (conveyor-\*) and messaging daemon (hermes) to send the events to ActiveMQ. There a script for that which repeats these daemons in single execution mode from the section in a loop::

    run_daemons


When all the daemons ran you will be able to find the events in Kibana. If you run the docker environment on you local machine you can access Kibana at http://localhost:5601. The necessary index pattern will be added automatically. There is also one dashboard available in Kibana. If it is running on remote machine you can SSH forward it::

    ssh -L 5601:127.0.0.1:5601 <hostname>


Additionally, there is also a Grafana server running with one simple dashboard. You can access it at http://localhost:3000. The default credentials are "admin/admin". Also ActiveMQ web console can be accessed at http://localhost:8161.

If you would like to continously create some transfers and events there are scripts available for that. Open two different shells and in one run::

    create_monit_data


And in the other run::

    run_daemons


Development
-----------

The idea for containerised development is that you use your host machine to edit the files, and test the changes within the container environment. Any change to files in your clone will be reflected into the containers by using volume mounts.

To see your changes in action the recommended way is to jump twice into the container in parallel. One terminal to follow the output of the Rucio server with a shortcut to tail the logfiles (`logshow`), and one terminal to actually run interactive commands:

From your host, get a separate Terminal 1 (the Rucio "server log show")::

    docker exec -it dev_rucio_1 /bin/bash
    logshow


Terminal 1 can now be left open, and then from your host go into a new Terminal 2 (the "interactive" terminal)::

    docker exec -it dev_rucio_1 /bin/bash
    rucio whoami


The command will output in Terminal 2, and at the same time the server debug output will be shown in Terminal 1.

[etc/docker/dev/README.rst:27-59] (relevance 0.01)
Now, ensure that the `.git/config` is proper, i.e., mentioning your full name and email address, and create the `.githubtoken` file that contains a full access token from `Github Account Settings <https://github.com/settings/tokens>`_.

Next, startup the Rucio development environment with docker-compose. There are three different types: a standard one to just run the unittests and do basic development, which includes just Rucio without any transfer capabilities. One slightly larger one, which includes the File Transfer Service (FTS) and three XrootD storage servers to develop upload/download and transfers capabilities. And a third large one, which adds the full monitoring stack with Logstash, Elasticsearch, Kibana and Grafana.

*Note: if you are running with SELinux enabled, you might run into problems. Check troubleshooting with SELinux on the help pages of your container runtime environment.*

Using the standard environment
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Run the containers using docker-compose (again might need `sudo`)::

    docker-compose --file etc/docker/dev/docker-compose.yml up -d

And verify that it is running properly::

    docker ps

This should show you a few running containers: the Rucio server, the PostgreSQL database and the Graphite monitoring.

Finally, you can jump into the container with::

    docker exec -it dev_rucio_1 /bin/bash

To verify that everything is in order, you can now either run the full unit tests or only set up the database. Running the full testing suite takes ~10 minutes::

    tools/run_tests_docker.sh

Alternatively, you can bootstrap the test environment once with the `-i` option and then selectively or repeatedly run test case modules, test case groups, or even single test cases, for example::

    tools/run_tests_docker.sh -i
    tools/pytest.sh test_replica.py
    tools/pytest.sh -vvv test_replica.py::TestReplicaCore
    tools/pytest.sh -vvv --full-trace test_replica.py::TestReplicaCore::test_delete_replicas_from_datasets

If you run the command below, the files are not in the RSE XRD3, but only in XRD1 and 2.::

    rucio list-file-replicas test:mynewdataset
    > +---------+--------+------------+-----------+------------------------------------------------+
    > | SCOPE   | NAME   | FILESIZE   | ADLER32   | RSE: REPLICA                                   |
    > |---------+--------+------------+-----------+------------------------------------------------|
    > | test    | file1  | 10.486 MB  | 141a641e  | XRD1: root://xrd1:1094//rucio/test/80/25/file1 |
    > | test    | file2  | 10.486 MB  | fdfa7eea  | XRD1: root://xrd1:1094//rucio/test/f3/14/file2 |
    > | test    | file3  | 10.486 MB  | c669167d  | XRD2: root://xrd2:1095//rucio/test/a9/23/file3 |
    > | test    | file4  | 10.486 MB  | 65786e49  | XRD2: root://xrd2:1095//rucio/test/2b/c2/file4 |
    > +---------+--------+------------+-----------+------------------------------------------------+


So let's add a new rule on our new dataset to oblige Rucio to create replicas also on XRD3::

    rucio add-rule test:mynewdataset 1 XRD3
    > 1aadd685d891400dba050ad43e71fea9


Now we can check the status of the rule. We will see there are 4 files in `Replicating` state::

    rucio rule-info 1aadd685d891400dba050ad43e71fea9|grep Locks
    > Locks OK/REPLICATING/STUCK: 0/4/0


Now we can run the daemons. First the rule evaluation daemon (judge-evaluator) will pick up our rule. Then the transfer submitter daemon (conveyor-submitter) will send the newly created transfers requests to the FTS server. After that, the transfer state check daemon (conveyor-poller) will retrieve from FTS the transfer state information. Finally, the transfer sign-off daemon (conveyor-finisher) updates the internal state of the Rucio catalogue to reflect the changes.::

    rucio-judge-evaluator --run-once
    rucio-conveyor-submitter --run-once
    rucio-conveyor-poller --run-once
    rucio-conveyor-finisher --run-once

    rucio list-file-replicas test:mynewdataset
    > +---------+--------+------------+-----------+------------------------------------------------+
    > | SCOPE   | NAME   | FILESIZE   | ADLER32   | RSE: REPLICA                                   |
    > |---------+--------+------------+-----------+------------------------------------------------|
    > | test    | file1  | 10.486 MB  | 141a641e  | XRD1: root://xrd1:1094//rucio/test/80/25/file1 |
    > | test    | file2  | 10.486 MB  | fdfa7eea  | XRD1: root://xrd1:1094//rucio/test/f3/14/file2 |
    > | test    | file3  | 10.486 MB  | c669167d  | XRD2: root://xrd2:1095//rucio/test/a9/23/file3 |
    > | test    | file4  | 10.486 MB  | 65786e49  | XRD2: root://xrd2:1095//rucio/test/2b/c2/file4 |
    > +---------+--------+------------+-----------+------------------------------------------------+


So let's add a new rule on our new dataset to oblige Rucio to create replicas also on XRD3::

    rucio add-rule test:mynewdataset 1 XRD3
    > 1aadd685d891400dba050ad43e71fea9


Now we can check the status of the rule. We will see there are 4 files in `Replicating` state::

    rucio rule-info 1aadd685d891400dba050ad43e71fea9|grep Locks
    > Locks OK/REPLICATING/STUCK: 0/4/0


Now we can run the daemons. First the rule evaluation daemon (judge-evaluator) will pick up our rule. Then the transfer submitter daemon (conveyor-submitter) will send the newly created transfers requests to the FTS server. After that, the transfer state check daemon (conveyor-poller) will retrieve from FTS the transfer state information. Finally, the transfer sign-off daemon (conveyor-finisher) updates the internal state of the Rucio catalogue to reflect the changes.::

    rucio-judge-evaluator --run-once
    rucio-conveyor-submitter --run-once
    rucio-conveyor-poller --run-once
    rucio-conveyor-finisher --run-once

Now, ensure that the `.git/config` is proper, i.e., mentioning your full name and email address, and create the `.githubtoken` file that contains a full access token from `Github Account Settings <https://github.com/settings/tokens>`_.

Next, startup the Rucio development environment with docker-compose. There are three different types: a standard one to just run the unittests and do basic development, which includes just Rucio without any transfer capabilities. One slightly larger one, which includes the File Transfer Service (FTS) and three XrootD storage servers to develop upload/download and transfers capabilities. And a third large one, which adds the full monitoring stack with Logstash, Elasticsearch, Kibana and Grafana.

*Note: if you are running with SELinux enabled, you might run into problems. Check troubleshooting with SELinux on the help pages of your container runtime environment.*

Using the standard environment
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~

Run the containers using docker-compose (again might need `sudo`)::

    docker-compose --file etc/docker/dev/docker-compose.yml up -d

And verify that it is running properly::

    docker ps

This should show you a few running containers: the Rucio server, the PostgreSQL database and the Graphite monitoring.

Finally, you can jump into the container with::

    docker exec -it dev_rucio_1 /bin/bash

To verify that everything is in order, you can now either run the full unit tests or only set up the database. Running the full testing suite takes ~10 minutes::

    tools/run_tests_docker.sh

Alternatively, you can bootstrap the test environment once with the `-i` option and then selectively or repeatedly run test case modules, test case groups, or even single test cases, for example::

    tools/run_tests_docker.sh -i
    tools/pytest.sh test_replica.py
    tools/pytest.sh -vvv test_replica.py::TestReplicaCore
    tools/pytest.sh -vvv --full-trace test_replica.py::TestReplicaCore::test_delete_replicas_from_datasets

Rucio - Scientific Data Management
==================================

Rucio is a software framework that provides functionality to organize, manage, and access large volumes of scientific data using customisable policies. The data can be spread across globally distributed locations and across heterogeneous data centers, uniting different storage and network technologies as a single federated entity. Rucio offers advanced features such as distributed data recovery or adaptive replication, and is highly scalable, modular, and extensible. Rucio has been originally developed to meet the requirements of the high-energy physics experiment ATLAS, and is continuously extended to support LHC experiments and other diverse scientific communities.

Documentation
-------------

General information, API/REST description and guides can be found in our `documentation <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation>`_ or on our `webpage <https://rucio.cern.ch>`_.

Try it out
----------

We provide a `dockerized environment <https://github.com/rucio/rucio/tree/master/etc/docker/dev>`_ which serves both as a demo environment and a development environment. It includes all the necessary preconfigured components for multiple storage and transfers developments.

Developers
----------

For information on how to contribute to Rucio, please refer and follow our `CONTRIBUTING <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation/contributing>`_ guidelines. We strongly recommend to use the `dockerized environment <https://github.com/rucio/rucio/tree/master/etc/docker/dev>`_ for development.

Operators
----------

To learn how to deploy and configure Rucio, consult the `documentation <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation>`_ available online.

Getting Support
----------------

If you are looking for support, join us on our Slack `support <https://rucio.slack.com/messages/#support>`_ channel, or send an email to our public mailing list `rucio-users@googlegroups.com <mailto:rucio-users@googlegroups.com>`_.

Rucio - Scientific Data Management
==================================

Rucio is a software framework that provides functionality to organize, manage, and access large volumes of scientific data using customisable policies. The data can be spread across globally distributed locations and across heterogeneous data centers, uniting different storage and network technologies as a single federated entity. Rucio offers advanced features such as distributed data recovery or adaptive replication, and is highly scalable, modular, and extensible. Rucio has been originally developed to meet the requirements of the high-energy physics experiment ATLAS, and is continuously extended to support LHC experiments and other diverse scientific communities.

Documentation
-------------

General information, API/REST description and guides can be found in our `documentation <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation>`_ or on our `webpage <https://rucio.cern.ch>`_.

Try it out
----------

We provide a `dockerized environment <https://github.com/rucio/rucio/tree/master/etc/docker/dev>`_ which serves both as a demo environment and a development environment. It includes all the necessary preconfigured components for multiple storage and transfers developments.

Developers
----------

For information on how to contribute to Rucio, please refer and follow our `CONTRIBUTING <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation/contributing>`_ guidelines. We strongly recommend to use the `dockerized environment <https://github.com/rucio/rucio/tree/master/etc/docker/dev>`_ for development.

Operators
----------

To learn how to deploy and configure Rucio, consult the `documentation <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation>`_ available online.

Getting Support
----------------

If you are looking for support, join us on our Slack `support <https://rucio.slack.com/messages/#support>`_ channel, or send an email to our public mailing list `rucio-users@googlegroups.com <mailto:rucio-users@googlegroups.com>`_.

[README.rst:1-29] (relevance 0.09)
Rucio - Scientific Data Management
==================================

Rucio is a software framework that provides functionality to organize, manage, and access large volumes of scientific data using customisable policies. The data can be spread across globally distributed locations and across heterogeneous data centers, uniting different storage and network technologies as a single federated entity. Rucio offers advanced features such as distributed data recovery or adaptive replication, and is highly scalable, modular, and extensible. Rucio has been originally developed to meet the requirements of the high-energy physics experiment ATLAS, and is continuously extended to support LHC experiments and other diverse scientific communities.

Documentation
-------------

General information, API/REST description and guides can be found in our `documentation <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation>`_ or on our `webpage <https://rucio.cern.ch>`_.

Try it out
----------

We provide a `dockerized environment <https://github.com/rucio/rucio/tree/master/etc/docker/dev>`_ which serves both as a demo environment and a development environment. It includes all the necessary preconfigured components for multiple storage and transfers developments.

Developers
----------

For information on how to contribute to Rucio, please refer and follow our `CONTRIBUTING <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation/contributing>`_ guidelines. We strongly recommend to use the `dockerized environment <https://github.com/rucio/rucio/tree/master/etc/docker/dev>`_ for development.

Operators
----------

To learn how to deploy and configure Rucio, consult the `documentation <https://rucio.cern.ch/documentation>`_ available online.

Getting Support
----------------

If you are looking for support, join us on our Slack `support <https://rucio.slack.com/messages/#support>`_ channel, or send an email to our public mailing list `rucio-users@googlegroups.com <mailto:rucio-users@googlegroups.com>`_.
